passage: When my mother, Kavitha, presses her lips into a thin line, I think she's angry. Last night she did it while reading a letter at the table, and I hid in my room for an hour, sure I'd done something. Finally I asked, “Are you angry with me?” She looked surprised. “No, Shalini. I'm just tired, and thinking about the guests coming.” I had worried for nothing. But once, when I broke a plate, the thin line was real. She said, “I was angry, and now I'm calm.” So I guess I'll always ask.

qa.q: What was Kavitha doing when she pressed her lips into a thin line last night?
qa.a: She was reading a letter at the table.

qa.q: What did Shalini think the tightened lips meant, and how did asking change her mind?
qa.a: She thought her mother was angry with her, so she hid in her room. When she asked, she learned her mother was just tired and thinking about the guests.

qa.q: What could Shalini do when she notices the thin line again?
qa.a: Ask a calm question, as she did last night, rather than hiding and guessing for an hour.

qa.q: How might Kavitha have felt when Shalini hid for an hour?
qa.a: Probably unaware at first, then surprised and perhaps a little sorry that her face worried her daughter. Her clear answer made things easier.

grounding: A child reads a parent's tightened lips as anger, sometimes right and sometimes wrong; a calm question helps.

passage: Note from Mahima, school counsellor. Sharmila told me she always knows when her father is angry because his lips go tight. Last week she was right: he had been shouted at by a customer at work. Yesterday she was wrong: he was just tired. She spent an evening avoiding him and felt worse. We practised one question she can ask calmly: “Are you upset with me, or just tired?” She said it aloud twice and laughed. I also told her that her father may not notice his face is doing it. She will try the question at home this week.

qa.q: What does Sharmila say her father's lips do when he is angry?
qa.a: She says his lips go tight.

qa.q: What was Sharmila probably feeling when she avoided her father yesterday, and why was she wrong?
qa.a: Probably worried he was angry with her, and it made her feel worse. She was wrong because he was just tired.

qa.q: What could Sharmila try at home this week?
qa.a: Ask the calm question they practised, “Are you upset with me, or just tired?”, instead of guessing from his lips.

qa.q: How might Sharmila's father feel if he learns she avoided him?
qa.a: He may be surprised and sorry that a tired face made her worry, and he may try to tell her when he is only tired.

grounding: A child reads a parent's tight lips as anger, sometimes correctly; a calm question helps.

passage: Friday night. Diary of Bhupen. Papa came home late and sat at dinner with his lips pressed into a thin line. Ma said, “Pankaj, eat something,” but he only nodded. I was sure it was about my report card, which is on the fridge with a C in science. I ate my whole plate without talking. When I put my plate in the sink, I asked quietly, “Papa, are you angry with me?” He looked up, surprised. “With you? No, beta. The bus broke down and I stood for two hours. I'm just very tired.” Then he looked at the fridge. “Science on Sunday. Not angry. Tired.” I slept better than I thought.

qa.q: What grade was on the report card on the fridge?
qa.a: There was a C in science on the report card.

qa.q: What was Bhupen feeling while eating without talking?
qa.a: Bhupen felt anxious and guilty, sure that Papa's pressed lips meant anger about the science grade.

qa.q: What did asking quietly achieve?
qa.a: It showed Papa was tired from the broken-down bus, not angry, and it set a calm time to talk about science.

qa.q: How was the evening for Pankaj?
qa.a: Pankaj was exhausted from standing for two hours and was surprised that his tired face looked angry to his child.

grounding: Shows a child reading a parent's tightened lips as held-back anger, and a calm question showing it was tiredness.

passage: Nikita carried the lunch tiffin down the field path and found her Baba, Omkar, standing still by the broken fence, lips pressed so tight they'd gone white. Nikita slowed. Last time he looked like that, he shouted at everyone for an hour. She set the tiffin on the bund and waited. Then she asked, “Baba, are you angry?” He let out a long breath. “Yes. Not at you. Someone's goats got in and trampled the new onion rows.” His lips loosened a little. “Help me put up thorn branches after lunch?” Nikita nodded and handed him the first roti.

qa.q: What did the goats trample?
qa.a: The goats trampled the new onion rows.

qa.q: What was Nikita feeling when she saw Baba's white, pressed lips?
qa.a: She felt nervous and wary, remembering the last time he looked like that and shouted for an hour.

qa.q: Why was waiting and then asking a good choice?
qa.a: It gave Omkar a moment to cool and a calm opening, so he could say he was angry but not at her, and ask for help.

qa.q: What was the morning like for Omkar?
qa.a: Omkar was angry about the trampled onions and holding it in, and felt some relief once he could say it aloud.

grounding: Shows a child correctly sensing restrained anger in a parent's tight lips, and a calm question showing it was not about her.

passage: In their kitchen in Stockholm, Lucia came in holding the vase she had just chipped. Her mother, Ingrid, sat at the table with a pile of forms, lips pressed flat, pen tapping. Lucia's heart sank. Mamma already looks furious, and she doesn't even know yet. Lucia nearly hid the vase behind her back. Instead she asked, “Are you cross?” Ingrid blinked up. “Cross? No, sweetheart. These school forms are just confusing, and I've been up since five.” Then she saw the vase. Her lips pressed again, for a second. “Ah. Tell me what happened.” Lucia did. It was only a small chip.

qa.q: What had Lucia chipped?
qa.a: Lucia had chipped the vase.

qa.q: What was Lucia feeling when she saw her mother's pressed lips?
qa.a: She felt scared and guilty, thinking Mamma was already furious before hearing about the chipped vase.

qa.q: What did asking “Are you cross?” make possible?
qa.a: It showed the tight lips came from confusing forms and tiredness, so Lucia felt safe enough to tell the truth about the vase.

qa.q: How did the morning feel for Ingrid?
qa.a: Ingrid was tired and focused on confusing forms, and her pressed lips were about concentration, not about Lucia.

grounding: Shows a child reading a parent's tightened lips as anger, and a calm question revealing tiredness and concentration instead.

passage:
In the Class 6 classroom, Nandini sat on a small chair next to Papa while Mrs Rao flipped through her notebook. "Three science assignments missing."

Papa's lips pressed into a thin, flat line. He said nothing, just nodded. Nandini's fingers went cold. He's furious. He'll shout the whole way home.

In the corridor, she couldn't bear it. "Papa, are you very angry?"

Kishore stopped and rubbed his eyes. "A bit, about the science. But mostly I came straight from the night shift, and my head is pounding." He squeezed her shoulder. "We'll make a homework chart tomorrow. Tonight, I sleep."

Nandini let out her breath.

qa.q: How many science assignments were missing?
qa.a: Three science assignments were missing.

qa.q: What did Nandini think Papa's thin, flat lips meant?
qa.a: She read them as held-back fury and felt frightened, expecting shouting all the way home; her cold fingers show the fear.

qa.q: Why did Nandini's question work well?
qa.a: Asking calmly let Papa explain that he was only a bit annoyed and mostly exhausted from the night shift, so she didn't have to guess.

qa.q: What was going on for Kishore behind the tight lips?
qa.a: Kishore was a little annoyed about the science but mainly worn out and in pain after the night shift, holding it together in the meeting.

grounding: It shows a child reading a parent's tightened lips as held-back anger, and a calm question revealing it was partly anger and mostly tiredness.
